id: A Secret Matter of Grave Importance

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Except when once we drew identical lots nothing’s ever come between us. We keep our drifts of space spare and daily shake our down. You’ve glanced beyond your dirty cuffs and caught me hand-washing my clean shirts. Stuck with sharp wind, both bloods are rare and rarely do we taste the walnut’s knot of oil. We wake between our fitted sheets and shake our fists or pretend real fright but not in this do we dare touch. My rib cage can stand in yours, yours become the swinging doors through which magician’s swords will slice and miss that knotted muscle. It is a trick. We’ll make an endless show of the outright clanking, irregular beating of our acrobatic hearts. We’ve designed the double bars of depth; our hearts skip — the tumbleset we think is absence, the somersault we call forbearance — the hearts are there, doing turns that teach us to count and keep each finger close to its own sly pulse.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Except, You, Stuck

outputs.L1:
Except for that one time we drew identical lots, nothing has ever come between us. We keep our separate spaces spare and, each day, shake down our bedding. You have glanced beyond your dirty cuffs and caught me hand-washing my clean shirts. Pierced by a sharp wind, both bloods are rare, and rarely do we taste the walnut’s knotted oil. We wake between our fitted sheets and shake our fists, or feign genuine fright; but even then, we do not dare to touch.

My rib cage can stand within yours; yours can become the swinging doors through which a magician’s swords slice and miss that knotted muscle. It is a trick. We will make an endless spectacle of the outright clanking, irregular beating of our acrobatic hearts. We have designed the double bars of depth; our hearts skip—the tumbleset we mistake for absence, the somersault we call forbearance—yet the hearts are there, turning and teaching us to count, and to keep each finger close to its own sly pulse.
outputs.L2: Only that one time, when we pulled matching lots, has anything ever stood between us. We leave the expanses around us mostly empty, and every day we fluff and settle our bedding. You have looked past your grimy cuffs and seen me washing my already clean shirts by hand. Pierced by a cutting wind, both kinds of blood are uncommon, and only seldom do we get the walnut’s tight knot of oil on our tongues. We rise inside our snug sheets and raise our fists, or act as though we are truly afraid, yet here we do not risk touching. My ribs can fit inside yours; yours can turn into swinging doors through which a magician’s blades pass, cutting through and still missing that knotted heart. It is an illusion. We will turn the blunt, metallic, uneven pounding of our agile hearts into a performance without end. We have built the twin rails of depth; our hearts miss a beat—the tumble we mistake for absence, the flip we name restraint—yet the hearts remain, turning over and over, training us to count and to keep every finger near its own secretive pulse.
outputs.L3:
The speaker describes an unusually close relationship, one in which very little has ever truly come between the two people. Their bond seems intimate and long-standing, yet it is not expressed through open affection or physical closeness. Instead, the relationship is defined by a carefully maintained emotional distance. Through ordinary daily habits, acts of restraint, and the deliberate avoidance of touch, the two people keep something unspoken but powerful under control.

Despite this distance, the speaker suggests that they are deeply alike. Images of blood, ribs, and hearts point to shared vulnerability and an almost bodily connection between them. These images imply that the two people are not separate in any simple way; they are linked by the same physical fragility and emotional intensity. Their closeness is internal rather than outwardly displayed.

The relationship is also presented as a kind of performance or trick. It involves danger, endurance, and precise control, as though both people are participating in an act that requires discipline and self-denial. They must appear calm and restrained, even though strong feeling exists beneath the surface. This sense of performance makes the relationship seem both impressive and precarious: it depends on balance, timing, and the ability to withstand pain without revealing too much.

Ultimately, the appearance of absence, silence, or forbearance does not mean that feeling has disappeared. Beneath the controlled surface, their hearts continue to beat, though irregularly and uneasily. The relationship is therefore marked by tension between closeness and distance, feeling and restraint, presence and apparent absence. What remains most powerful is not what is openly shown, but what continues to live beneath the surface.
outputs.L4:
Intimacy in the text is not presented as simple closeness, nor distance as simple separation. Instead, the relationship between the two figures exists in a strange and delicate space where nearness and restraint continually overlap. They are deeply linked, almost physically or instinctively synchronized, yet they remain guarded. Their vulnerability is real, but it is not offered openly or easily. It appears through indirect gestures, surreal images, and carefully controlled movements, as though the body itself must invent metaphors in order to express what ordinary language cannot.

The text uses bodily imagery to make emotional experience feel physical and uncanny. Feelings are not merely described; they are transformed into acts of balance, concealment, tension, and exposure. The body becomes a stage on which intimacy is performed, but also protected. This creates the sense that love is both deeply felt and carefully managed. The people at the center of the text do not simply confess themselves to one another. They reveal themselves through discipline, timing, and restraint, as if any sudden movement might break the fragile structure that holds them together.

Metaphors of performance, magic, and acrobatics deepen this idea. Performance suggests that love involves roles, gestures, and an awareness of being seen. Magic suggests secrecy, illusion, and the possibility that what appears to be missing may actually be present in another form. Acrobatics suggests risk: the lovers, or the two connected figures, must trust one another while remaining suspended in a difficult and unstable position. Their bond depends on precision. One person’s movement affects the other’s balance. What looks effortless may in fact require enormous concentration.

Because of this, absence in the text does not simply mean emptiness, and silence does not simply mean lack of feeling. Restraint becomes a form of communication. Distance becomes another way of maintaining connection. The emotional presence between the two people is hidden, but not weak. It is complex, disciplined, and synchronized, operating beneath the surface like a private choreography. Their love is not loud or openly sentimental; it is measured, guarded, and deeply attentive.

Ultimately, the text presents love as an act of balance. To love, in this vision, is not only to reach toward another person, but also to know when to hold back. It is to remain connected without collapsing the necessary space between two selves. Through its surreal bodily images and theatrical metaphors, the text reveals that intimacy can exist inside distance, and that vulnerability can survive even when it is carefully concealed. What first appears to be absence or emotional restraint becomes, on closer reading, a powerful form of presence: a hidden connection maintained through trust, discipline, and delicate mutual awareness.
outputs.L5:
Everyone seemed to move on with their lives, changing with the seasons as if it were easy. The streets filled with new faces, old buildings turned into cafés, and even the memories that once felt heavy began to fade.

Except you.

You stayed in my mind like a song I couldn’t stop hearing, like a door left half open in an empty house. No matter how far I walked or how busy I became, some part of me remained stuck in the moments we never finished. I tried to let time do what time is supposed to do, but it only softened the edges—it never erased you completely.

Maybe that is what it means to miss someone: not to stop living, but to carry a quiet place inside you where nothing changes. A place where the world moves forward, except you, still there, still remembered, still stuck between goodbye and everything I never said.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, surreal prose poem about twins or lovers whose closeness is expressed through physical distance, domestic rituals, and acrobatic heart imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
At breakfast we sit at opposite ends of the table to prove the table is one body. You butter the morning in the north; I salt the egglight in the south. Between us the spoons lie in a silver flock, migrating nowhere. We do not touch. Touch would be too small an animal for us. Instead you lift your cup and I feel my mouth become warm; I fold the napkin and your ribs remember wings.

We are twins, perhaps, or lovers misfiled by the moon, born from one door and leaving by two different walls. Each evening we widen the room by standing apart: you in the laundry’s damp cathedral, I beneath the stove’s blue hymn, both of us listening to the same heart practice its impossible gymnastics. It vaults from my chest to yours, a red acrobat over the clothesline, landing barefoot on a chair, bowing to the onions, somersaulting through the dark cupboard where our dead cups sleep.

Our rituals keep us distant enough to remain joined. You sweep the floor into constellations. I wash the knives until they forget murder. You hang shirts like pale ghosts along the hallway; I button my shadow into each one. At midnight we lie in separate rooms and turn, turn, turn—two keys in the same invisible lock. The house exhales around us. The pipes recite our blood in opposite directions.

Once, crossing the yard, I saw your heart balancing on the roof ridge, arms out, trembling, radiant, while mine below held the ladder in its teeth. Neither climbed. Neither fell. This is how we survive intimacy: by making a circus of absence, by letting the red trapeze swing empty between us, by trusting the catch to the air.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental paragraph in the style of contemporary lyric poetry, using second person plural, about intimacy, restraint, and two hearts performing like circus acts.
counterfactuals.output: You keep your hands folded in your laps like trained birds, though the room keeps asking for wings; you speak softly, as if desire were a glass balanced on a seal’s nose, as if one wrong syllable could spill the whole bright animal. Inside you, your two hearts climb the same narrow ladder in sequins and fear, leap through hoops of flame, bow to the silent crowd of all you will not say. You smile with your mouths closed. You practice restraint until it resembles tenderness. Above you, the trapeze swings empty, back and forth, back and forth, and still you know: if either of you reaches, both of you will fly.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a single paragraph of abstract literary prose that sounds like a translated modernist poem, centered on two people with “acrobatic hearts” and the illusion of absence between them.
counterfactuals.output: Between them there was said to be a distance, but it was only the illusion of absence, a curtain painted with roads, winter stations, unanswered rooms; they stood on either side of it with their acrobatic hearts, those small red trapeze artists, leaping and catching in the dark without applause, and if one turned away the other felt the air tilt, felt the invisible rope tremble under the weight of a name not spoken. They had never been simple bodies, no, but two weather systems translated badly into flesh, two lamps exchanging darkness, two exiles who discovered that separation is sometimes only another form of touch, stretched thin, made ceremonial, made cruel by mirrors. In the city, the clocks opened and closed like tired mouths; in the fields, grass rehearsed the green grammar of return. Yet they remained there, impossibly near, each carrying the other like a hidden architecture, while the world, with its official maps and obedient doors, insisted on the empty space between them.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an original prose poem about siblings or partners who share mirrored lives, using vivid bodily imagery, domestic details, and a tone that is intimate, uncanny, and difficult.
counterfactuals.output:
We were born in opposite rooms of the same house.

You came out red and furious, fist clenched around nothing. I arrived quiet, blue-lipped, already listening for you through the wall. Our mother said the plaster sweated that night. Our father boiled towels in a dented pot and left the stove on until morning. Ever since, everything in our lives has happened twice, but never in the same direction.

When you cut your thumb on the bread knife, I tasted iron. When I broke my tooth on a cherry pit, you pressed your tongue to the empty socket in your own sleep. We learned to sit at the kitchen table with our elbows touching, two bowls of soup steaming between us like small weather systems, each spoon rising as the other descended. Salt on your wrist, pepper under my nail. The refrigerator clicked and hummed and kept our secrets cold.

At night we lay in separate beds, head to foot, so that if one of us dreamed of drowning, the other woke with wet ankles. You kept a jar of buttons on your dresser; I kept a jar of baby teeth. Neither collection was complete. In winter, our hands cracked in the same places. In summer, the backs of our knees bloomed with the same rash. We were not twins exactly, not lovers exactly, not ghosts, though people used all those words when they wanted us to stop looking at them.

We grew older in the manner of a house: slowly, by damage. Your hair darkened as mine went pale. I learned to darn socks and make coffee strong enough to stand a spoon in. You learned to leave. Still, each evening, wherever you were, my sink filled with your dirty cups. A ring of your mouth on the glass. Your soap softening in my dish. Your coat hanging from my chair, heavy with rain from a city I had never entered.

Once, you telephoned after midnight and said, I think I am becoming you. I was already awake, holding the receiver, hearing my own breath return from far away with your lungs around it. Outside, the laundry on the line lifted and collapsed, lifted and collapsed, like a row of pale ribs.

We tried to separate properly. We divided the spoons, the photographs, the dead. You took the mirror from the hallway; I kept the nail where it had hung. For months I saw myself only in windows at night, doubled over the black glass, one face behind another. For months you wrote letters addressed to me in your own handwriting and signed them with my name. I did not answer, but my body did: a bruise opening on my thigh, milk souring in my mouth, the old scar at my wrist warming like a stove eye.

Now we live on opposite sides of the same silence.

In my house, the kettle screams each morning. In yours, perhaps, a cup waits under the leak in the ceiling. I fold sheets alone and find your shape in them, long and stubborn, smelling faintly of sleep. Sometimes I press my ear to the pantry door and hear you swallowing. Sometimes you must lift your shirt and see my heart moving under your skin, not where it belongs, but where it insists.

Do not come home, I tell you.

Come home, says the mirror, fogged by my breath.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
